endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Additional questions include whether IRB approval and FDA submissions may be required for future application of the AI solution, and whether integration of the AI tool requires disclosures on the interface or consent from patients.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Have transparency, disclosure, and outcome-proxy measures been defined before enabling AI functionality?

endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: Critical to the successful adoption of AI is identifying partners and subject matter experts who can support your health center’s AI development process. Experienced partners can include vendors, leaders from Health Center Controlled Networks (HCCN) and Clinically Integrated Networks (CIN), internal staff, and other health centers with relevant AI experience.

endorsements.title: When time is of the essence: ethical reconsideration of XAI in time-sensitive environments
endorsements.quote: Should stakeholders determine that an XAI architecture still is the optimal choice for decision support in the clinical setting, they are advised to conduct a more thorough examination of the clinical context to ascertain the extent to which the explanations provided by the system can enhance clinical judgement within the specific field of deployment.

endorsements.title: Artificial intelligence governance framework for healthcare
endorsements.quote: Embedding these types of assessment mechanisms in the governance process allows for a more thorough understanding of the AI system being implemented, and most importantly, one that is aligned with the organizations values.

endorsements.title: Transparency and Authority Concerns with Using AI to Make Ethical Recommendations in Clinical Settings
endorsements.quote: Nevertheless, given that the problems with transparency and authority are entirely foreseeable, institutional leaders have an obligation not to proceed down this path without first being able to adequately address these concerns.

endorsements.title: Tribulations, Triumphs, and Governance: Shaping the Future of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
endorsements.quote: Transparency and Accountability: Mandate full disclosure of model architecture, training datasets, and decision-making processes to support auditability and clinician trust.

endorsements.title: From frailty-driven to frailty-informed care in the age of wearable AI
endorsements.quote: Finally, transparency regarding which features are available to clinicians and patients, and what level of explainability is required for genuinely informed decision-making, should be specified prospectively as part of system design rather than inferred at the point of care.

commentary.bottom_line: Eight sources endorse defining transparency measures before enabling AI and reassessing explainability at each review, but no supplied study tests the practice or documents the hazard. The recommendation currently rests on two CHAI frameworks, one action guide, and five commentaries.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests whether pre-specified transparency measures or lifecycle explainability reviews change clinician understanding, error rates, or patient outcomes. The support consists of two CHAI frameworks, one action guide, and five commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not establish certainty of effect, so the rating is no direct evidence.

One commentary on time-sensitive care advises teams to examine the clinical context before relying on explanations. This suggests that explainability criteria may need to differ by workflow rather than apply uniformly. No supplied study measures the staff time, fidelity, or workflow effects of running these assessments at adoption and at each review.

The CHAI guide ties transparency review to questions about IRB approval, FDA submission, interface disclosure, and patient consent. The endorsing sources present the practice as voluntary governance and do not identify a legal mandate. None of the supplied material reports whether such reviews alter adoption decisions or regulatory filings.

The Action Guide is written for community health centers and their controlled networks, which indicates interest from safety-net settings. No supplied study examines whether transparency criteria include plain-language or translated disclosures, or whether explanations are understood by patients with limited English proficiency or low health literacy.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems that define transparency and explainability criteria before enabling AI with systems that do not. Useful studies would measure clinician comprehension of outputs, appropriateness of overrides, error detection, patient understanding of disclosures, and the staff time each review requires, and would report results for safety-net and limited English proficiency populations.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The Action Guide targets community health centers, but whether transparency criteria serve patients who need translated or plain-language explanations remains unexamined.
